analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run public health insurance option alongside private plans on the ACA exchanges.
analysis.headline: A bill to let Americans buy into a government-run public health insurance option was referred to committee and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The CHOICE Act would have created a government-administered public health insurance plan offered nationwide on the ACA marketplaces alongside private insurers, with bronze, silver, and gold tiers [S2]. It would compete on the same terms as private plans, but HHS could set doctor, hospital, and drug payments at Medicare rates when negotiation failed, and doctors participating in Medicare or Medicaid would be enrolled unless they opted out [S2, S3]. It was never taken up by the Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: People buying insurance on the ACA marketplaces, and the uninsured, would gain a public plan that could undercut private premiums by using Medicare payment rates and lean administration. Providers would gain a new national payer.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directed HHS to offer a public health insurance plan nationwide through the ACA exchanges, in bronze, silver, and gold tiers, giving consumers a plan to compare against private insurers.

Where HHS could not negotiate provider or drug rates, the plan would pay at Medicare rates, and the plan had to fully finance itself through premiums, mechanisms aimed at keeping premiums lower than private plans.
An ombudsman office and optional state advisory councils of consumers and providers were created to handle complaints and advise on the plan's operations.

analysis.who_pays: Private insurers would face a new government competitor, and hospitals and doctors would face payment rates that could be set at Medicare levels. Taxpayers would front start-up funding, repayable over ten years.

drawbacks.text: The public option would pay doctors and hospitals at negotiated rates with Medicare rates as the fallback, which providers argued could underpay hospitals and push some clinics to limit participation or shift costs elsewhere.

The plan was required to fully finance its own benefits and administrative costs through premiums plus a contingency margin, so its savings depended on it actually achieving lower costs; if it underperformed, the government would bear the shortfall risk since insurance risk could not be shifted to contractors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is a cheaper public insurance alternative nationwide; the main cost is disruption for private insurers and administrative start-up risk for the government, plus the concern that doctors and hospitals could face Medicare-level payments across the board. On balance the bill would have lowered health costs for many families, and it died without any hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 24, 2017, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
No further action was recorded: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
The bill attracted 40 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support; committee consideration was controlled by the House Republican majority.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and provider interests are better off, since no public competitor to their exchange plans was created. Americans who might have chosen a cheaper public plan never got the option.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers; no public option exists

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the CHOICE Act to create a public health insurance option.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee or floor consideration; the Energy and Commerce Committee, where it was referred, took no recorded action.

sides.party_line_note: All 40 cosponsors were Democrats, including every original sponsor, and the Republican-led committee and majority never moved the bill [S4, S5].

industries.note: The public option would have competed directly with private insurers on the exchanges, likely with lower premiums and administrative costs. Insurers no longer faced that competition because the bill never advanced.

Providers would have been enrolled in the public option by default unless they opted out, and it could have paid them at Medicare rates where negotiation failed, which provider groups have historically opposed.
Drug reimbursement under the public option would be negotiated by HHS, falling back to Medicare rates, a lever for lower drug prices that private plans lack.
